verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 3.75% to 4.00%. This is a close call. A rise is a very real possibility.
verdict.confidence_note: “Low” means this is close to a coin flip. A single report, the September price report due tomorrow (October 14), could be enough to change our answer.
verdict.short_version: The Fed has already said it plans to raise rates again. The real question is when. We think it will more likely wait until December than act in October.
verdict.card_why: Inflation at 3.4% argues for another rise, but weak September hiring and a jump in bond yields let the Fed wait for December.

why_steps.title: The Fed has two jobs, and one main tool
why_steps.html: By law, the Fed tries to do two things at the same time: keep prices steady and keep jobs plentiful. For prices, its target is that things should cost about 2% more each year, which is slow enough that people barely notice. Its main tool is its interest rate, the cost of borrowing money. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas: loans get cheaper, spending picks up, and companies hire more. Holding means keeping your foot where it is.

why_steps.title: Right now, prices are the bigger problem
why_steps.html: Prices are rising about 3.4% a year, measured by the Fed's preferred price gauge, called PCE (the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost $100 a year ago now costs about $103.40. The goal would be about $102. The main cause is energy. Conflict in the Middle East pushed up oil prices this year. Regular gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon in mid-October, compared with roughly $3.12 a year earlier. Energy matters for everything, because trucks carry food to shops, factories run machines, and airlines burn fuel, so higher energy costs slowly spread into the price of almost everything. Fed officials point out that prices have now been above the 2% goal for more than five years, and they worry people will start to expect high inflation as normal.

why_steps.title: So in September the Fed pressed the brake
why_steps.html: On September 16 the Fed raised its rate by 0.25 percentage points, to 3.75%–4.00%. All 12 voters agreed. In their written forecasts, 16 of the 18 Fed officials said they expect to raise rates at least once more before the end of 2026, and 4 of them expect two more rises. There are only two meetings left this year: October 28 and December 9. So the next rise will most likely come at one of those two. The question is which one.

why_steps.title: Reasons the Fed might wait until December
why_steps.html:
• Hiring has slowed sharply. Only 29,000 jobs were added in September, and July was revised to a loss of 10,000 jobs. When hiring is weak, pressing the brake again right away raises the risk of layoffs.
  • The market already pressed the brake for them. The interest rate on 10-year U.S. government bonds rose from 5.00% to 5.21% in less than a month. Mortgages and many business loans follow that rate. So borrowing has already become more expensive, which cools the economy without the Fed doing anything.
  • Senior officials hinted there is no rush. Governor Christopher Waller said rate rises do not need to come at consecutive meetings. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said reaching a decision may take more time.
  • The brake takes time to work. A rate change takes many months to fully affect the economy. The Fed only raised six weeks ago and may want to see the effect first.
  • Important reports come out just after the meeting. The first official look at summer economic growth and the September PCE price report are both released on October 29, the day after the decision. December's meeting will have all of this, plus two more jobs and price reports and fresh forecasts.

why_steps.title: Reasons the Fed might raise in October anyway
why_steps.html:
• Inflation is too high and not improving. Meeting notes say progress has been insufficient and that the risk is of prices going higher, not lower.
  • The economy is strong enough to handle it. Shoppers spent 0.8% more in September than in August, and an Atlanta Fed model estimates the economy grew at about a 3.6% yearly pace this summer. A strong economy can absorb a higher rate.
  • Many officials want insurance. Meeting notes say many officials think raising earlier is safer than waiting, in case inflation proves stubborn.
  • The Fed has made a public promise. Its statements emphasize that the Committee will deliver price stability. Acting sooner can make that promise more believable.

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

right: “No rush” hints from Waller and Jefferson

why_steps.html: Both sides are strong. What tips us slightly toward Hold is that the Fed itself has said timing is flexible, and December gives it more information at almost no cost. That is why we say about 55% Hold and 40% Raise, not something more lopsided.

why_steps.title: The one thing to watch: tomorrow's price report
why_steps.html: On Wednesday, October 14, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes September's Consumer Price Index (CPI), a monthly measure of the prices families pay. CPI is not the Fed's official target (that is PCE), but it comes out first and moves in a similar direction, so the Fed watches it closely. If core prices (prices without food and energy, which jump around a lot) rise 0.4% or more in one month, we would likely switch our main call to Raise. A calm reading of 0.2% or less would make us more confident in Hold.

timeline.title: The Fed cut its rate three times
timeline.what: The Fed lowered its rate by 0.25 points in September, October and December 2025, taking it from 4.25%–4.50% down to 3.50%–3.75%.
timeline.why: Hiring had slowed, and the Fed worried that people could start losing jobs. Inflation looked like it was slowly coming under control, so the Fed felt safe pressing the gas a little.
timeline.people: Borrowing got a bit cheaper (for example on credit cards and car loans), and interest earned on savings accounts dipped.
timeline.because: the Fed decided to pause and watch. Rate cuts take months to work, so it wanted to see their effect before doing more.

timeline.title: A pause: the rate stayed at 3.50%–3.75%
timeline.what: The Fed held its rate. Its statement described inflation as somewhat elevated and said job gains had remained low. Two voters wanted another cut.
timeline.why: The Fed was balancing two worries: jobs were soft, but prices were still a little too high. Holding was the middle path.
timeline.people: Not much change. Loan and savings rates stayed about the same. At this point, most debate was about when to cut again, not about raising.
timeline.because: the Fed was sitting still when a new problem arrived: trouble in the Middle East started pushing up energy prices.

timeline.title: An energy shock: prices start climbing again
timeline.what: The Fed held in March and April. In April it said inflation was elevated in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices. Three voters objected to the statement still hinting at future cuts.
timeline.why: When oil gets expensive, it does not just raise gasoline prices. It raises the cost of shipping, farming, flying and making things, so prices across the economy creep up.
timeline.people: Filling the car and heating the home got noticeably more expensive. Families with lower incomes and people in rural areas, who drive more, felt it most.
timeline.because: the mood inside the Fed shifted. Instead of asking when do we cut?, officials began asking should we stop talking about cuts at all?

timeline.title: A new leader at the Fed
timeline.what: Kevin Warsh became Chair of the Fed. The previous Chair, Jerome Powell, stayed on the Board as a Governor.
timeline.people: Nothing changed immediately, but markets paid close attention to how the new leadership would respond to rising prices.
timeline.because: the next meetings were led by a new Chair, facing the same energy-driven price problem.

timeline.title: Still holding, but pressure to raise grows
timeline.what: In June all 12 voters agreed to hold, and the statement added a firm line: The Committee will deliver price stability. In July the Fed held again, but this time three voters wanted to raise the rate.
timeline.why: Prices kept running hot. The hint about future cuts was gone, replaced by a promise to bring prices down. Some officials felt that words were not enough and action was needed.
timeline.people: The chance of cheaper loans soon faded. Savers kept earning similar rates. Bond markets started to expect rate rises.
timeline.because: everyone watched the August data closely to see whether prices would calm down on their own. They did not.

timeline.title: Prices hot, spending strong, jobs okay
timeline.what: Consumer prices (CPI) were up 3.7% from a year earlier, with energy alone up 20.4%. The Fed's preferred gauge (PCE) was also up 3.4%, and 3.0% without food and energy. Shop sales jumped 0.8% in September. The economy grew at a 2.2% yearly pace in spring.
timeline.people: Paychecks were rising about 3% a year, roughly the same as prices, so many families felt they were running just to stand still.
timeline.because: the Fed concluded that waiting was no longer enough.

timeline.title: The Fed raised its rate to 3.75%–4.00%
timeline.what: The first rise in this cycle, by 0.25 points. All 12 voters agreed. The Fed said this will support a timelier return to 2% inflation.
timeline.people: Rates on credit cards and many variable loans went up a little. Savings accounts and short-term deposits started paying slightly more.
timeline.because: investors expected more rises to come, so longer-term borrowing costs in the market rose too.

timeline.title: Market interest rates jumped
timeline.what: The interest rate on 10-year U.S. government bonds (often called the 10-year Treasury yield) rose from 5.00% to 5.21%. The 2-year rate rose from 4.80% to 4.79%.
timeline.why: When investors expect the Fed to keep rates high and prices to stay high, they demand more interest to lend money for years at a time.
timeline.people: Mortgage rates and many business loan rates follow the 10-year rate, so buying a house or expanding a business got more expensive within weeks.
timeline.because: the economy started to feel tighter even without another Fed move. Some officials began saying they could take their time.

timeline.title: A weak jobs report for September
timeline.what: Only 29,000 jobs were added. Unemployment ticked up from 4.1% to 4.2%. But weekly claims for unemployment benefits stayed very low (199,000).
timeline.people: If you have a job, it is fairly safe. If you are looking for one, it has become harder to find.
timeline.because: the case for raising rates again right away became weaker, because pressing the brake too hard on a slowing job market is risky.

timeline.title: What Fed officials said after the rise
timeline.because: our reading is raise again, but maybe not in October, which is why our main call is Hold, with Raise close behind.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 3.75%–4.00%
choices.meaning: the Fed keeps its foot where it is on the brake. It would likely say it still expects to raise later, so a hold here would be a not yet, not a never.
for: Weak hiring. September added only 29,000 jobs. The Fed does not want to cause layoffs by braking too hard, too fast.
The market did some of the work. Higher bond rates already make mortgages and business loans dearer, which cools spending in the same way a Fed rise would.
Officials signalled patience. Waller said rises need not come at back-to-back meetings. Jefferson said a decision may take more time.
The September rise needs time to work. It has only been six weeks.
December is a better moment. The Fed will have the summer growth number, the September PCE price report, two more jobs reports and fresh forecasts.
against: Inflation is far from the goal. At 3.4% vs 2%, and the Fed itself calls progress insufficient.
Most officials expect another rise. 16 of 18 wrote down at least one more this year. Waiting could look like hesitation.
The economy looks strong. If growth is near 3.6%, the economy can handle a higher rate now.
A hot price report on October 14 could make waiting feel too risky.
choices.everyday: loan and savings rates would stay roughly where they are for now. Markets would then focus on December, where a rise would still be widely expected.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 4.00%–4.25%
choices.meaning: the Fed presses the brake a little harder, for the second meeting in a row, to show it is serious about bringing prices down.
for: Prices have been too high for over five years. Officials worry people will start to see high inflation as normal, which makes it harder to fix.
Energy is still expensive. Oil is near $96 a barrel and gasoline about $4.33 a gallon, so price pressure is still feeding through.
Insurance. Meeting notes say many officials prefer to act early, in case inflation proves stubborn.
The promise. Delivering price stability is a strong public commitment. Acting quickly backs it up.
Spending is strong. Shop sales jumped 0.8% in September, so demand is not fading on its own.
against: Hiring is weak. Two rises in a row while job growth is near zero could push companies to start cutting staff.
Officials said timing is flexible. They have openly said rises do not need to happen at every meeting.
October has no new forecasts. The Fed often prefers to make moves at meetings where it also publishes updated projections, like December.
choices.everyday: credit card and other variable loan rates would rise a little further. Savings accounts would pay a bit more. Mortgage rates could rise further if markets expect even more rises after that.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate
choices.meaning: the Fed would switch from the brake to the gas, reversing its September decision.
for: Only in an emergency: for example a sudden market crash, a financial firm getting into serious trouble, or a sharp jump in layoffs before the meeting.
Even then, the Fed would more likely hold first than cut straight away.
against: The Fed just raised. Cutting six weeks later would confuse people and damage its credibility.
Nobody is asking for it. In the speeches and statements we read since September, no official argued for a cut.
Inflation is moving the wrong way. Cutting would add fuel to rising prices.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but the surprise itself would likely signal that something had gone badly wrong in the economy.

change.lead: Our 55% / 40% / 5% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Some of it can move our view a lot. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro_title: Why before and after the meeting matters
change.intro: The Fed can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before October 28 can change the October decision. A report released after it can only shape what happens in December. That is why the reports in the first part of the table matter most right now.

producer_price_index_ppi.why: Business costs today often become shop prices a few months later. It is an early warning.
producer_price_index_ppi.trigger: A big jump would add to the case for Raise.

retail_sales.why: If spending stays strong, the economy can handle a higher rate, and demand keeps pushing prices up.
retail_sales.trigger: Another gain of around 1% or more → leans Raise. A drop → leans Hold.

weekly_jobless_claims.why: The fastest signal of layoffs. Right now it is very low (about 199,000).
weekly_jobless_claims.trigger: A steady climb toward 250,000 or more → Hold firms up, and cut talk could start.

housing_starts.why: Housing reacts first to higher mortgage rates. A sharp fall would show the brake is already biting.

durable_goods_orders.why: Shows whether businesses are still investing heavily.

gdp_q3_first_estimate_pce_pric.why: Too late for October, but key for December.

employment_cost_index.why: Fast pay growth can keep service prices high.

jobs_report.why: Will show whether September's weak hiring was a one-off.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Energy is the main driver of today's inflation. A new jump in oil (for example well above $100 a barrel) would make a rise more likely. A big drop would make waiting easier.
Bond market rates. One of our main reasons for Hold is that market rates already rose. If the 10-year rate falls back sharply, that reason weakens and Raise becomes more likely.

Final words from Fed officials. Officials stop giving policy speeches shortly before each meeting (a quiet period). That usually begins about 10 days before, so around October 17. Anything they say before then is the last direct hint we get.
A financial shock. A sudden market fall or trouble at a big financial firm would almost certainly push the Fed to hold, and could even raise the chance of a cut.

report_card.one: Things cost 3.4% more than a year ago, far above the 2% goal.
report_card.look: The Fed's preferred price gauge (PCE, up 3.4%), the same gauge without food and energy (core PCE, up 3.0%), and consumer prices (CPI, up 3.7%).
report_card.why: The Fed's official measure (PCE) is well above the goal, both with and without energy, and prices have been above target for over five years. Energy is up 20.4% in a year. Business costs (PPI) are up 5.4%, which can reach shop shelves later. Fed officials themselves say the risk is that prices go higher still.
report_card.change: Several months of core prices rising 0.2% a month or less, and energy prices falling back.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason the Fed is raising rates at all. As long as this stays red, the Fed leans toward pressing the brake.

report_card.one: Few people are losing jobs, but companies are hiring slowly.
report_card.look: New jobs each month, the unemployment rate, weekly claims for unemployment benefits, and job openings.
report_card.why: Good news: unemployment is low at 4.2%, and weekly layoff claims are very low (199,000). Bad news: only 29,000 jobs were added in September, July showed a loss, and few workers are quitting to switch jobs, which shows low confidence. It is not bad enough to be red, but not healthy enough to be green.
report_card.change: Rising layoff claims or a jump in unemployment → red. Hiring picking back up above 100,000 a month → green.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason the Fed might wait. A weak job market makes another rate rise riskier.

report_card.one: The economy is growing at a solid pace, and people are still spending.
report_card.look: GDP (gross domestic product, the total value of everything the country produces), consumer spending and retail sales.
report_card.why: The economy grew at a 2.2% yearly pace in spring, and an Atlanta Fed model estimates about 3.6% for summer. Shop sales jumped 0.8% in September. Businesses are investing heavily, especially in artificial intelligence. One caution: people are spending more than their incomes are growing, and their saving rate is low at 4.1%.
report_card.change: A sharp drop in spending or a weak official summer GDP number on October 29 → yellow.
report_card.matters: A strong economy can handle higher rates. This gives the Fed room to raise without much fear of causing a recession (a period when the economy shrinks).

report_card.one: Borrowing costs jumped, but lenders are still lending calmly.
report_card.look: U.S. government bond rates (Treasury yields), the extra interest risky companies pay to borrow (credit spreads), and market expectations for inflation.
report_card.why: Worrying: the 10-year bond rate rose from 5.00% to 5.21% in under a month, making mortgages and loans more expensive. Reassuring: risky companies still borrow easily (spread of 3.16%, which is low), and investors still expect inflation of only about 2.35% a year over the long run.
report_card.change: Credit spreads widening sharply or stock markets falling hard → red. Bond rates settling down → green.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates are already slowing the economy, which is one reason the Fed may wait. Calm long-term inflation expectations mean the Fed does not need to panic.

consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.what: the government checks the prices of thousands of everyday things, like food, rent, gasoline, clothes, and doctor visits, and compares them with a year ago. A 3.7% rise means a $100 shopping basket now costs about $103.70.
consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.why: it is the most-watched price report in the country because it comes out first each month. It is 1.7 points above where the Fed wants prices to be. The 0.6% jump in just one month (September) is worrying, because if that pace continued for a year, prices would rise much faster.

core_cpi_without_food_and_energy.what: the same price check, but with food and energy removed. Those two jump up and down with weather, wars and harvests, so economists take them out to see the slower, steadier trend underneath.
core_cpi_without_food_and_energy.why: on a yearly basis this looks fairly calm at 2.6%, which shows the problem is mostly energy. But the monthly rise of 0.3% is a little fast. The Fed's fear is that expensive energy slowly leaks into everything else.

cpi_energy.what: the price of gasoline, heating oil, electricity and natural gas for households.
cpi_energy.why: this is the main reason overall prices are high. A 20.4% jump in a year is very large. Energy also feeds into other prices, because almost every product has to be made, moved or kept cold or warm using energy. If energy calms down, overall inflation should calm down too, which is what the Fed is hoping for.

cpi_shelter_housing_costs.what: the cost of rent, and an estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their own home.
cpi_shelter_housing_costs.why: housing is the biggest single cost for most families, about a third of the CPI basket. A 3.2% rise is not alarming, but it is not low enough to help pull overall inflation down to 2%.

pce_prices_the_fed_s_official_target.what: the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, from the Commerce Department. Like CPI, it tracks prices, but it covers a wider range of spending (including things paid for on people's behalf, like employer health insurance) and adjusts when people switch to cheaper products.
pce_prices_the_fed_s_official_target.why: this is the number the Fed's 2% goal is actually based on. At 3.4%, it is 1.4 points above target. When the Fed says inflation is too high, this is the number it means.

core_pce_without_food_and_energy.what: the Fed's official price measure, with food and energy removed to show the underlying trend.
core_pce_without_food_and_energy.why: many economists consider this the Fed's favourite gauge. At 3.0%, it is still a full percentage point above the goal, even after removing energy. That tells the Fed the problem is not only energy.

producer_price_index_ppi_final_demand.what: prices that businesses charge each other, for example what a factory charges a shop, or what a trucking company charges a supermarket.
producer_price_index_ppi_final_demand.why: businesses usually pass higher costs on to customers, often a few months later. A 5.4% rise in business costs is an early warning that shop prices could keep rising.

10_year_inflation_expectation_from_bon.what: by comparing two kinds of government bonds (one protected against inflation and one not), we can work out how much inflation investors expect on average over the next 10 years.
10_year_inflation_expectation_from_bon.why: this is good news at 2.35%. Investors still believe inflation will settle near 2–2.5% in the long run. That means people trust the Fed to fix the problem eventually. If this number started rising quickly, it would be a big warning sign and the Fed would likely act faster.

new_jobs_nonfarm_payrolls.what: the change in the number of people on company and government payrolls (farm jobs are counted separately). It comes from a large monthly survey of employers.
new_jobs_nonfarm_payrolls.why: 29,000 is very low for an economy this size. It is the strongest reason the Fed might wait in October, because raising rates when hiring is this weak could tip companies into cutting jobs.

unemployment_rate.what: the share of people who want a job, and are actively looking, but do not have one.
unemployment_rate.why: 4.2% is still low by historical standards, and Fed officials consider it close to maximum employment. A small rise is not a crisis, but if it kept climbing the Fed would become much more cautious.

average_hourly_pay.what: the average hourly wage for workers.
average_hourly_pay.why: pay is rising about 3.0% while prices are rising faster, so many workers are slowly losing buying power. For the Fed, this is also a sign that wages are not the main cause of inflation.

labour_force_participation.what: the share of all adults who are either working or looking for work.
labour_force_participation.why: at 61.8%, it is steady, which suggests the low unemployment rate is genuine and not caused by people dropping out.

weekly_jobless_claims_new.what: how many people applied for unemployment benefits for the first time in a given week.
weekly_jobless_claims_new.why: at 199,000, this is very low. It shows companies are holding on to workers even though they are not hiring many new ones.

continuing_jobless_claims.what: the number of people still receiving unemployment benefits.
continuing_jobless_claims.why: at 1,710,000, if this keeps rising while new claims stay low, it means people who lose jobs are taking longer to find new ones, which matches the low hiring picture.

job_openings_jolts.what: the number of jobs companies are trying to fill, from the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey.
job_openings_jolts.why: at 7.1 million, there are still many open jobs, which supports workers. But the number is slowly falling, a sign that demand for workers is cooling.

quit_rate.what: the share of workers who quit their job in a month, usually to take a better one.
quit_rate.why: at 1.9%, workers are nervous. It also means less pressure for employers to raise pay, which helps keep inflation down.

real_gdp_growth_spring.what: GDP (gross domestic product) is the total value of everything the country produces. Real means the effect of price rises is removed. 2.2% is the yearly pace at which the economy was growing in spring.
real_gdp_growth_spring.why: about 2% is considered healthy and normal for the U.S. The summer number arrives on October 29.

gdpnow_model_estimate_summer.what: a computer model run by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta that estimates GDP before the official number is released.
gdpnow_model_estimate_summer.why: 3.6% would be strong growth. If correct, it supports the view that the economy can handle another rate rise.

retail_sales.what: total sales at shops, restaurants, petrol stations and online stores, before removing price changes.
retail_sales.why: consumer spending is about two-thirds of the U.S. economy. A 0.8% monthly rise means demand is still pushing prices up.

real_consumer_spending.what: how much more people actually bought, after taking out the effect of higher prices.
real_consumer_spending.why: at +0.6% in the month, it shows people were not just paying more, they were buying more.

real_after_tax_income.what: the money people have left after taxes, adjusted for price rises.
real_after_tax_income.why: at −0.0% in the month, spending grew but income did not. People cannot keep spending more than they earn forever.

personal_saving_rate.what: the share of after-tax income that people save instead of spend.
personal_saving_rate.why: 4.1% is low. It means families are stretching their budgets, likely because of high energy costs.

fed_s_target_range_federal_funds_rate.what: the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed sets a range and keeps the actual rate inside it.
fed_s_target_range_federal_funds_rate.why: this is the main pedal the Fed controls. Almost every other interest rate moves with it.

effective_federal_funds_rate.what: the actual average rate banks paid each other for overnight loans, published each business day by the New York Fed.
effective_federal_funds_rate.why: at 3.88%, it confirms the Fed's target is working as intended.

3_month_treasury_bill.what: the interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow for three months.
3_month_treasury_bill.why: at 4.26%, it is higher than the Fed's rate. That gap tells us investors expect the Fed to raise rates within the next few months.

2_year_treasury_yield.what: the interest the government pays to borrow for two years.
2_year_treasury_yield.why: at 4.79%, this rate is mostly driven by what investors think the Fed will do over the next two years.

10_year_treasury_yield.what: the interest the government pays to borrow for ten years. It is one of the most important interest rates in the world.
10_year_treasury_yield.why: at 5.21%, mortgage rates and many business loans follow this rate. It makes buying homes and expanding businesses more expensive, which slows the economy on its own.

30_year_treasury_yield.what: the interest the government pays to borrow for thirty years.
30_year_treasury_yield.why: at 5.56%, it shows the long-term cost of government borrowing.

high_yield_credit_spread.what: the extra interest that riskier companies pay to borrow, on top of what the government pays.
high_yield_credit_spread.why: at 3.16%, it is low, which means lenders are calm and businesses can still borrow.

fed_officials_end_2026_rate_forecast_d.what: four times a year, each of the 18 Fed officials writes down where they think the rate should be at the end of the year. The middle answer is called the median.
fed_officials_end_2026_rate_forecast_d.why: at 3.6%, it shows that officials expect further adjustments over time.

futures_market_odds_of_a_rise_by_decem.what: investors trade contracts that pay out based on future Fed rates. Governor Waller quoted futures traders seeing about an 85% chance of at least one rise by December.
futures_market_odds_of_a_rise_by_decem.why: markets strongly expect a rise by December, but this tells us nothing about October alone.

oil_price_wti_crude.what: the price of a barrel of U.S. crude oil, the raw material for gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
oil_price_wti_crude.why: at $96.24, oil near $100 keeps energy prices, and therefore overall inflation, high.

u_s_gasoline_regular.what: the average price at the pump across the country.
u_s_gasoline_regular.why: at $4.331 a gallon, it hurts family budgets and shapes how people feel about inflation.

european_central_bank_deposit_rate.what: the main interest rate for the euro area.
european_central_bank_deposit_rate.why: at 2.50%, it is much lower than the U.S. rate.

bank_of_england_rate.what: the main interest rate in the United Kingdom.
bank_of_england_rate.why: at 3.75%, the UK is holding steady for now.

said.pv: July: held, vote 9–3 (3 wanted a rise)
w: What it said: inflation remains elevated and the rise will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
Why it matters: the Fed moved from talking to acting. A unanimous vote shows broad agreement inside the Fed that prices are the priority.

said.v: Most expect another rise by year-end
w: What it is: a detailed summary of the discussion at the meeting, published three weeks later. It does not name who said what.

Why it matters: it shows most officials think another rise is likely this year, that many want insurance against stubborn inflation, and that each meeting is open. The phrase by year-end rather than at the next meeting is part of why we lean toward December.

said.v: further policy adjustments are likely to be needed
w: What he said: inflation risks have grown while job market risks have eased, so policy needs adjusting.
Why it matters: he expects more rises but did not say when. It supports the idea that the next move is up, not down.

said.v: Inflation too high for too long
w: What she said: she supported the September rise and wants to bring inflation down while keeping the job market strong. She gave no timing.
Why it matters: her balanced tone suggests she is not pushing for a rush, but she is clearly focused on inflation.

said.v: A decision may take more time
w: What he said: bond rates have risen further since September, and the Fed will need to come to its own judgment.
Why it matters: the Vice Chair is the Fed's second-in-command, so his words carry weight. This is one of the clearest hints that the Fed may not move in October.

said.v: The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings
w: What he said: he expects more rises if the data come in as expected, but there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.

Why it matters: Waller has been an influential voice. He clearly expects more rises, and just as clearly says they do not have to happen at the very next meeting. This is the single strongest reason behind our Hold call.

gaps: Market odds for October alone. We found no official source. Governor Waller quoted futures traders seeing about an 85% chance of at least one rise by December, but no October number. Why it matters: we cannot compare our 40% chance of an October rise with what markets expect.
Chair Warsh's own words. We could not load his September press conference transcript, so we do not quote him. Why it matters: the Chair's tone is often the best single hint about the next move.
Regional Fed bank presidents' speeches (for example Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) were not collected. Why it matters: several of them vote this year and were early to push for rises.
Summer (Q3) economic growth is not officially out until October 29. The 3.6% figure is an Atlanta Fed model estimate, not the official number.
Business surveys (ISM), consumer surveys (University of Michigan), mortgage rates, and the Bank of Japan's latest decision were not collected.
The date of the European Central Bank's last rate change, and the Fed's other administered rates (such as the rate paid on bank reserves), were not checked.
Fed meeting notes mention an upcoming change in how some PCE prices are measured, which could lower recent readings. We did not confirm the details.
How we gathered data: a web search tool was not available for this build. Every number was read directly from the official page linked next to it.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The Fed's goal is about 2% a year, measured by PCE. CPI is a similar measure that comes out earlier each month. It is closely watched, but it is not the Fed's formal target.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether people can find and keep work, the Fed's second job. A weak job market makes the Fed more careful about raising rates.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing and whether people are still spending. A strong economy can handle higher interest rates. A weak one cannot.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the Fed's own rate and the rates set by investors in financial markets. Market rates often move before the Fed does, because investors try to guess the Fed's next step.
group_intros.said: Fed officials often hint at what they will do next. Reading their words carefully is one of the best ways to guess the next decision.
group_intros.global: The U.S. economy is affected by what happens elsewhere, especially energy prices and what other central banks do.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the Fed has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the Fed must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 13, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.
